, the ATLAS detector will undergo upgrades to its softron collider to improve data collection efficiency. The resulting increase in data volume will strain the ATLAS computing grid's capacity, prompting an upgrade to high-performance computing centers. This infrastructure will process large datasets in remote areas, managing data locally before transmitting results to central servers. A key challenge will be optimizing the data transfer between local and grid resources, particularly with network outages and variable bandwidth. Our study examines the effectiveness of two strategies - transferring full dataset segments and incremental segments - to minimize data transfer disruptions and reduce overall transmission time. We evaluated these approaches in a simulated high-energy physics context, using a full ATLAS dataset replica, and found that the incremental method yields significant time savings, particularly in environments with fluctuating network bandwidth. This method also minimizes data transfer disruptions, ultimately resulting in a 30% reduction in overall transmission time compared to traditional methods. This finding has important implications for the future operation of high-energy physics computing grids. Additionally, the techniques employed in this study can be adapted for use in other high-energy physics computing contexts. Experiments on various image classification tasks demonstrate that our method achieves an average accuracy of 0.9, outperforming previous methods by 0.1, and results in a notable reduction of 50% in parameters and a 30% decrease in inference time.  The implementation of our method is made publicly available.  The findings of our study are also used to develop an interactive app that showcases the impact of pruning on image classification models.  Mobile users can upload their images, view the pruned network's structure, and observe the resulting accuracy and inference time. A sophisticated attack can be launched by embedding a trigger pattern into input data, causing the DNN to misclassify inputs with this trigger as the desired class while maintaining high accuracy on normal inputs. To address this issue, this research proposes an innovative two-stage defense strategy that combines a trigger detector with a reinforcement learning-based classifier. The trigger detector is trained to identify backdoor triggers in input data, and its output is used to contaminate samples with low confidence, effectively neutralizing the attack. The reinforced learning module is then trained to classify these contaminated samples accurately. Our experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this two-stage defense strategy in countering backdoor attacks. We believe that this research is the first to employ reinforcement learning as a countermeasure and sets a new benchmark in the field of backdoor defense. Historically, semijoin queries have been optimized through techniques like joining the relation to itself or using indexes, but these approaches are not always effective due to the high volume of data being processed. ReAct has been shown to outperform other algorithms in the tested benchmark, highlighting its potential as a powerful tool for continual learning. In this study, we investigate methods to better comprehend the decision-making processes of deep neural networks by analyzing the influence of individual input components on their predictions. We introduce a new approach called Deep Local Effect Analysis (DLEA), which can be applied to various neural network types. Our approach is compared to existing techniques, such as LIME and CEE, in terms of their ability to explain model decisions. Furthermore, we examine the robustness of these explanations in the presence of noisy input data. Our findings suggest that explanations derived from DLEA and CEE models are more resilient to noise compared to those generated by LIME. This study highlights the potential of DLEA as a superior explanation method, particularly in scenarios involving noisy data. We provide our code to facilitate future research.

Subsequently, we identify the Galois closure as the largest cover preserving the Galois correspondence, and we demonstrate that it is both uniquely determined and computable. Additionally, we prove the existence of a Galois closure for every Galois homomorphism between tropical curves that are Galois covers of a common parent. Furthermore, we develop a Galois correspondence for the direct product of Galois covers, and we generalize the Galois closure to the direct product of individual covers. Building upon this Galois closure, we introduce a Galois closure for the direct product of Galois homomorphisms between tropical curves that are Galois covers of a common parent. Finally, we investigate the existence of a Galois closure for the direct product of Galois homomorphisms in relation to the existence of a Galois closure for the individual homomorphism, and we examine the relationship between the Galois closure of the direct product and the direct product of the Galois closures. Notably, we find that the Galois closure of the direct product is the direct product of the Galois closure of the individual homomorphism. This work is an extension of a previously developed theory of Galois covers for curves that are homeomorphic. The "subhalo abundance matching" technique, which connects dark matter halos to galaxies, is a prominent approach that relies on a particular mass function.  However, the mass function used in this method is based on a simplified model that does not accurately account for the complexity of dark matter halo formation. This work highlights the need for developers to be cautious when handling blockchain failures and user data.
